name: Amira Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, AI firms or political parties. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a shovel, the big machine that scoops rock into haul trucks, at a large iron ore mine. At 43 I'm one of the people called when the loading face looks wrong, and my technical diploma helps with the drawings as much as the machine. My partner cleans at a clinic, and we've two school-age children and a mortgage; after the car repairs we've less than a month of expenses saved. This mine pays towards the bottom for the job, with few others close enough to commute. I like teaching a new driver to watch the ground, but I need somebody to prove new software works before I trust it; I've only used AI occasionally to help rewrite a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good if the office can stop making us enter the same load twice. I'd still want a person checking the ground before the shovel moves. There's no prize for saving ten minutes and losing a machine in a soft patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm more worried about the car needing another repair than about this small amount of AI. If I can't get to the mine, I don't earn, and the mortgage doesn't wait. Being experienced hasn't turned this into a well-paid mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the shovel shifts and the walk around the loading face before work. Starting this payday I'll put 20 a week into a separate car account. Through the first year I'd keep doing that rather than treating a quiet AI story as spare spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about money, although work itself feels familiar. Last month I watched the temperature gauge all the way up the mine road. I don't want the car's red temperature needle deciding whether the children get their school trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make the car saving stick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd make the car money the first thing to leave my pay, not whatever is left on Sunday. My partner agreed we could cut the bought lunches to cover most of it. I wouldn't promise a huge emergency fund when we haven't managed a small one yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the routine AI tools in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try a simple form tool once another shovel operator had used it without losing records. I'd ask for a demonstration during work, then compare the result with our normal sheet. I want fewer forms, not a new argument about a missing load.

say: I welcome **less duplicate entry**, provided somebody still checks the ground before moving the shovel.
I want **reliable records**, rather than a faster form that loses track of an actual load.
think: I worry about **car repairs** stopping me reaching the mine and keeping up with the mortgage.
I know **experience** has not raised this mine's low pay or created another nearby employer.
do: Keep the **shovel shifts** and walk around the loading face before work each day.
Put **20 weekly** into a car account from payday, funded mainly by bringing lunch.
feel: I feel **anxious** about another car repair while the hands-on work itself still feels familiar.
S0.quote: I don't want the car's red temperature needle deciding whether the children get their school trip.
fieldNote: Her existing **transport risk** makes AI Plateau financially anxious despite little reason to expect the shovel job to disappear.
She is willing to test a **proven tool**, but wants a demonstration and a comparison with records she already understands.

steps.text: Keep shovel shifts and check the loading face before work
Transfer 20 weekly into the separate car repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we should test the new planning with our own shift records. If fewer office staff can do the paperwork, I'd want the savings to pay for learning time on the machines. I wouldn't call every change a trick, but I'd ask who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the shovel still needing me while planning and ordering change sooner. What worries me is the company expecting the same people to do more loading and more checks in fewer paid hours. Losing a weekend shift would hurt us more than losing a form would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll join the operators' meeting and ask for paid time to practise the new planning display after a trial crew has checked it. In the first year I'll compare my actual hours each month with the old rota. I'll also keep putting the 20 a week aside for the car, because I still need to reach whichever shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, with a bit of interest in whether the paperwork could improve. I don't expect a robot shovel next week in this picture. I do think our hours could shrink while management says nothing has really changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask one experienced driver and one newer driver to try the display, not just a supervisor. If both can explain why it chose a loading order, I'd give it a turn. A neat screen isn't proof of a safe shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision at home would you delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we should hold off replacing the fridge until we've seen three months of shift sheets. Ours makes a terrible noise but still keeps food cold. I'd rather listen to the fridge than ask the lender for an extension over an avoidable purchase.

say: I want **operators involved** in a real trial before planning changes become everyone's responsibility.
I would ask whether **paperwork savings** can pay for proper learning time on the machines.
think: I expect **planning work** to change sooner than my shovel, but shorter paid shifts could still reach us.
I worry that **extra checks** will come with fewer hours while managers describe the change as minor.
do: Attend the **operators' meeting** and seek paid practice after a trial crew checks the display.
Compare monthly **shift hours** and keep adding 20 a week to the car account.
feel: I feel **anxious** about hours, with some interest in tools that might remove duplicate paperwork.
S1.quote: A neat screen isn't proof of a safe shift.
fieldNote: She separates **early planning changes** from slower robot adoption and focuses on how a smaller rota could reduce household income.
Her acceptance depends on a **credible trial** involving ordinary drivers; cautious interest does not remove her concern about paid hours.

steps.text: Attend the operators meeting to request paid display practice
Keep adding 20 weekly to the car repair account
Delay replacing the household fridge until three months of shift sheets arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company needs to show us a people plan alongside the equipment plan. AGI in 2028 can change the planning, and robots around 2031 can take the shovel work too. I'd ask the union to negotiate before the orders are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose a large part of my wage once the shovel can run without me. Two years to thinking AI and then three more to robots is some warning, but our savings are measured in weeks. I keep waking up wondering whether the house would have to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union this month to bargain for paid machine-maintenance training and wages during the training. Starting now we'll freeze the fridge purchase and keep the car reserve. In the first year after AGI arrives I'll take a proven maintenance course if the mine offers a paid place, rather than spend our reserve on an advertised promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, because I can picture the wage going and I can't yet replace it. There are still steps I can take, and I'd take them. That doesn't stop me counting mortgage payments at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the risk at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that the plan is uncertain rather than pretend my seniority protects us. We'd work out the smallest income that keeps the mortgage and school costs covered. My partner's cleaning pay matters, but it doesn't replace a mining wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you need before accepting training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see former operators actually doing the maintenance job after training. I need to know the hours and pay, not just that the course has a smart name. My mortgage needs a real vacancy at the end of a training course.

say: I want a **people plan** negotiated before the company orders equipment that removes loading jobs.
I would ask the **union** to bargain over wages and paid training, not just the machine timetable.
think: I expect a **large wage loss** when robots can operate the shovel around 2031.
I know **weeks of savings** cannot carry the mortgage through a long unpaid course or job search.
do: Ask the **union** to negotiate paid maintenance training and wages during the course.
Freeze the **fridge purchase** and take only a proven paid training place after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and wake at night counting mortgage payments, although I still have actions to pursue.
S2.quote: My mortgage needs a real vacancy at the end of a training course.
fieldNote: The expected **loss of earnings** and disturbed sleep support alarm despite her composed account and clear sequence of actions.
Her concern about **training outcomes** reflects thin savings and a cautious learning style, rather than blanket opposition to changing work.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid maintenance training
Freeze the fridge purchase while calculating essential household costs
Take a proven paid maintenance course if the mine offers a place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years ought to buy a proper training rota, not five years of rumours. Planning changes in 2031, and robots around 2034 give operators a later deadline. I'd still want our union involved in who gets those training places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the fast picture, a cheaper shovel without a driver threatens my wage. The difference is I could finish a course and build some savings while I still have shifts. I'd be about 51 when robots arrive, so I need a job afterwards rather than an early retirement dream.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a trial maintenance placement next year, after speaking to operators who have done it. We'll put 40 a month into a separate emergency account as well as the car money, using the cancelled fridge replacement. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd apply for a maintenance vacancy if the trial and training have gone well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I feel more useful to my own family in this version. Five years gives us time to make a mistake on a small trial and correct it. I don't have to bet the mortgage on the first course advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a small maintenance trial look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for one day alongside the maintenance crew before committing to the full course. I know worn parts from operating, but repair work has other skills and I don't want to fake them. If it doesn't suit me, I'd know while I still have a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the savings plan meets another car repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra 40 for a month if the car broke, rather than borrow to pretend we'd met a target. Saving needs to work in the household we have. Five years lets me try a new job while my old wage still pays for supper.

say: I want a **training rota** and fair access to places during the five-year warning.
I would keep the **union involved** in decisions about which operators can move into maintenance.
think: I still expect **driverless shovels** to threaten my pay, but can test another role before losing shifts.
I need **another wage** after 2034 because I would be about 51 when robots arrive.
do: Request a **maintenance trial** after hearing directly from operators who have completed one.
Save **40 monthly** beyond the car reserve and apply for a maintenance vacancy after successful training.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with enough warning to test a change without gambling our whole reserve.
S3.quote: Five years lets me try a new job while my old wage still pays for supper.
fieldNote: A longer horizon permits a **reversible trial**, matching her preference for evidence before committing to unfamiliar work.
She keeps the **savings plan flexible** around car repairs, avoiding a fictional large cushion built from an already stretched wage.

steps.text: Request a supervised maintenance trial before committing to the full course
Put 40 monthly into an emergency account beyond the car reserve
Apply for a maintenance vacancy after successful trial and training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew ten years means we can insist on gradual changes that people can actually follow. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 is a long timetable, but I'd still want dates for training. A promise without a first day is easy to postpone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be about 56 at the robot stage and the children would be adults. That reduces some costs, but I can't assume the mortgage or my need to earn has vanished. I could become comfortable in maintenance over that time, provided there's a real path into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for the maintenance trial next year rather than waiting for 2036. If it works, I'll finish the paid course over several years and apply for openings as they come. In the first year after AGI arrives I'd keep the car and emergency accounts intact while checking whether my new role is itself changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about the eventual wage change, though I don't have the same tight feeling in my chest. The long warning gives me room to learn at a sensible pace. I still wouldn't call a single employer and thin savings secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children over that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that they can explore different subjects, and that my job isn't a promise for their future. I wouldn't frighten them with a deadline at dinner. We'd review their study costs as they grew, without signing for a bigger house now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance itself be protected from AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the maintenance crew how much diagnosis or ordering has already moved to software. Switching jobs doesn't mean escaping every change. I want to learn a different part of the mine, not buy a story that another job is safe forever.

say: I would press for **training dates** now rather than let a long warning become a reason to delay.
I want **gradual learning** that operators can follow while still doing their existing shifts safely.
think: I would still need **earnings at 56**, even with grown children and potentially lower household costs.
I know **maintenance can change** too, so a new job would need continued attention rather than blind trust.
do: Start the **maintenance trial** next year and complete a paid course gradually if it fits.
Apply for real **maintenance openings** and preserve both reserves while reviewing changes after AGI arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** about eventually replacing my wage, with less physical dread and more time to practise.
S4.quote: I want to learn a different part of the mine, not buy a story that another job is safe forever.
fieldNote: She uses the decade for **gradual skill building**, without assuming either automatic retirement or permanent protection in a different role.
Her caution extends to **future maintenance tasks**, showing that her plan is a practical option rather than a claim to predict employment.

steps.text: Start a maintenance trial next year and complete suitable paid training
Apply for maintenance openings after gaining practical experience
Preserve separate car and emergency reserves while reviewing household costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the one that keeps me up, because the main wage could go while our reserve is still tiny. A paid course with a genuine job at the end would help more than a list of websites. I can learn, but I need time to practise without putting the house on the line.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the journey to work. A course that starts when my night shift ends, miles away, might as well be closed to me. Somebody needs to ask operators when we can actually attend.

headlineQuote: I can learn, but I need time to practise without putting the house on the line.
portrait: Amira is a **43-year-old shovel operator** with a technical diploma, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
A **car repair** can unsettle a household with less than one month saved and few nearby mining employers.
She accepts **proven changes**, using trials and experienced colleagues to judge tools before committing to new ways of working.
Longer warnings make **paid maintenance training** more workable, though she still expects to need earnings when robots reach the mine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove the main wage before the family has a useful reserve or replacement job.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid practical training** with genuine vacancies and hours that shift workers can actually attend.
